newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Kidnap-murder erodes public confidence in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Kidnap-murder erodes public confidence in Taiwan.

text.p: The murder of a Taiwan actress's teenage daughter, whose body was found on Monday, has left residents wondering if the government is capable of protecting them.

The murder and kidnapping 17-year-old, Pai Hsiao-yen, daughter of popular actress Pai Ping-ping, follows a spate of violence on the wealthy island, from gangland-style executions to the assassination of a government official.
Analysts said on Tuesday the violence is eroding confidence in the government's ability to stem the recent rise in crime.
And fears have reached the highest levels, with the wife of Premier Lien Chan telling the local daily China Times Express on Tuesday she was afraid her children would be kidnapped.
Late on Monday, police found the body of Pai Hsiao-yen floating in a river in Taipei county. She was naked, her hands and legs bound by rope.

The teenager, also a daughter of the late Japanese best-selling comic book artist Ikki Kajiwara, was kidnapped on April 14 on her way to school and had been dead for at least eight days, coroner Yang Jih-sung said. She had been strangled.

The kidnappers had chopped off half of the victim's left little finger, sent it to her mother and demanded a US$5 million ransom. Her mother had wanted to pay the ransom, but the kidnappers aborted a planned meeting.

The case has shocked the island nation of 21 million, with President Lee Teng-hui saying he was "extremely saddened" and "outraged by the criminals' inhuman method", the Presidential Office said in a statement.
"Authorities had mobilised an unprecedentedly large number of police in this case, but they couldn't save the victim," said Chu Hai-yuan, a sociology researcher at Academia Sinica.
He said the public has lost their confidence in the government's ability to maintain law and order.
"If the government has no power to tackle a security crisis, it should apologise to the public and leaders like the premier, interior minister and national police chief should step down," he said.
The sharp rise in crime includes the assassination of a local government official and seven others last November in a gang-style execution.

Several days later, a prominent opposition feminist went missing on her way to a party congress. Her naked body was found three days later with 35 knife wounds and she had apparently been sexually assaulted, police said.

Lee Ching-tan, a law professor of Tunghai University, blamed Taiwan's notorious "black money politics", referring to infiltration of gangsters into local politics, as the cause of a rapid deterioration of law and order in Taiwan.

"'Black money' has seriously polluted our politics ... and damaged our law and order," he said, adding the government must eradicate such practice to "return the public the right to live without fear".

An opinion poll published by the United Daily News on Tuesday showed that 81 percent of 800 residents interviewed often worried that they or their family members would be hurt or kidnapped by gangsters.
The same poll showed that 28 percent of the respondents planned to emigrate.
Taiwan reported 156 kidnapping cases in 1996, the highest number since 1990, the state-run Central News Agency said.
Government statistics have also shown an average 15,000 Taiwan residents have emigrated in each of the past three years.
On Tuesday, Fang Yu, wife of Lien Chan, added her voice to growing fears over public safety.
"I knew it put pressure on my husband when I said that, but whenever my children came home a little late, I was very, very worried," she said.
